title: Protein Biochemistry
objectives: Understand the structural hierarchy of proteins from primary to quaternary structure
Describe the chemical and physical properties of amino acids and their impact on protein function
Explain protein folding, stabilization forces, and denaturation processes
Analyze the relationship between protein structure and function with clinical examples
Understand protein synthesis, post-translational modifications, and degradation pathways

overview.title: Protein Structure Fundamentals
overview.content:
Proteins are complex macromolecules composed of amino acid polymers that perform virtually all cellular functions. They serve as enzymes, structural components, signaling molecules, transporters, and antibodies. Proteins exhibit four levels of structural organization that determine their function, with precise folding being essential for biological activity.

Structural Hierarchy

  • Primary Structure: Linear sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds
  • Secondary Structure: Local folding patterns (α-helices, β-sheets) stabilized by hydrogen bonds
  • Tertiary Structure: Overall 3D conformation stabilized by various interactions
  • Quaternary Structure: Assembly of multiple polypeptide chains into functional complexes

Key Properties

Chemical Characteristics

  • Amphoteric nature (isoelectric point)
  • UV absorption at 280 nm (aromatic residues)
  • Charge distribution (electrophoretic mobility)
  • Hydropathy index (membrane association)

Physical Properties

  • Molecular weight (SDS-PAGE analysis)
  • Solubility (salting in/out effects)
  • Thermodynamic stability (ΔG of folding)
  • Cooperativity (allosteric transitions)

structural_biology.title: Structural Determinants
structural_biology.content:
Stabilizing Forces

Covalent: Peptide bonds, disulfide bridges (Cys-Cys)

Non-covalent: Hydrogen bonds, ionic interactions, van der Waals forces, hydrophobic effect

Metal Coordination: Zinc fingers, calcium-binding motifs

Motifs and Domains

Supersecondary Structures: βαβ units, Greek keys, β-hairpins

Functional Domains: SH3 domains, immunoglobulin folds, kinase domains

Quaternary Assemblies: Homo/hetero-oligomers, viral capsids

Folding Pathways

Anfinsen's Dogma: Native structure determined by amino acid sequence

Chaperones: HSP70, HSP60 (GroEL/GroES) systems

Folding Landscapes: Energy funnels and molten globule states

functional_biochemistry.title: Functional Mechanisms
functional_biochemistry.content:
Enzyme Catalysis

Active Sites: Precise spatial arrangement of catalytic residues

Mechanisms: Acid-base, covalent, metal ion catalysis

Kinetics: Michaelis-Menten parameters, Lineweaver-Burk plots

Allosteric Regulation

Models: MWC (concerted) vs. KNF (sequential)

Examples: Hemoglobin (O2 binding), ATCase (feedback inhibition)

Membrane Proteins

Types: Integral (GPCRs), peripheral (annexins), lipid-anchored (G-proteins)

Structural Features: Transmembrane helices, β-barrels, pore domains

dynamics_processing.title: Dynamics and Processing
dynamics_processing.content:
Synthesis and Maturation

Translation: Ribosomal synthesis, signal sequences

PTMs: Phosphorylation, glycosylation, ubiquitination

Processing: Proteolytic cleavage (zymogens), disulfide formation

Conformational Changes

Switches: GTP-binding proteins, calcium sensors

Mechanotransduction: Fibronectin, titin elasticity

Degradation Pathways

Ubiquitin-Proteasome: Targeted destruction of misfolded proteins

Autophagy-Lysosomal: Bulk degradation of organelles

clinical_correlations.title: Clinical Correlations
clinical_correlations.content:
Folding Disorders

Amyloidoses: Alzheimer's (Aβ), Parkinson's (α-synuclein)

CFTR: ΔF508 mutation in cystic fibrosis

Enzyme Deficiencies

PKU: Phenylalanine hydroxylase deficiency

Lysosomal Storage: Tay-Sachs (hexosaminidase A)

Therapeutic Targets

Protease Inhibitors: HIV antiretrovirals

Monoclonal Antibodies: Cancer immunotherapy

faqs.title: FAQs
faqs.content:
Why does protein denaturation lead to loss of function?+
Denaturation disrupts the precise 3D structure required for functional sites, destroying catalytic activity and binding specificity while keeping primary structure intact.
How do chaperones assist protein folding?+
Chaperones provide isolated environments (like GroEL cavity) and use ATP-driven conformational changes to prevent aggregation and allow proper folding.
What determines whether a protein will form α-helices vs β-sheets?+
Secondary structure depends on amino acid sequence - helix formers (Ala, Leu, Glu) vs strand formers (Val, Ile, Thr), and local backbone dihedral angles (φ/ψ in Ramachandran plot).
Why are intrinsically disordered proteins functional despite lacking stable structure?+
Disorder enables binding promiscuity (multiple partners) and dynamic regulation, often undergoing folding upon binding (coupled folding-binding).
